I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 16:30 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T23:30:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 40.07 degrees and its azimuth is 254.785 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 46.927 degrees and its azimuth is 214.747 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 6.51 percent illuminated, 29.501 degrees from the Sun, and 372194.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely.

The Moon is **46.9° above the horizon**, toward azimuth **214.7°** (southwest), while the Sun is at azimuth **254.8°** (west-southwest) and altitude **40.1°**. So the Moon is about **30° away from the Sun**, high enough to be well clear of horizon haze.

At **6.5% illumination**, it will be a thin waxing crescent, and daylight makes it lower-contrast than at dusk. But its angular separation from the Sun is comfortably large, and its altitude is excellent. With clear skies and normal vision, you should be able to see it **without optical aid**, especially if you first use the Sun’s position to orient yourself and then scan about **30° toward the south**—roughly **two fist-widths at arm’s length**—and about **7° higher**.

Do **not** look near the Sun directly. If you have trouble, binoculars can help locate it, but only use them after ensuring they cannot sweep across the Sun.
